What was missing with your experience with us?

1) I would have liked some more information up front with regard to some of the details of the course. I only found out the exam date after I was registered (and that it was a set time), and some of the initial material seemed to conflict on whether the course was 6 or 8 or 10 weeks. I'm not sure if I missed the communication somewhere, but it could perhaps be more explicit as closed vs open book does impact the way one prepares and studies. 

2) Some of the time estimates at the start of each module (5-7 hours) don't feel accurate, given the volume of reading. Some of the modules have 60+ pages of "core" reading, plus a few hundred pages of additional required reading plus videos. I don't think it's possible to properly study this amount of material within 7 hours. 

3) I think the start of each module should be more explicit in managing expectations around time and volume by, for example, specifying that there are x many pages of core reading, plus y pages of additional reading plus z minutes of videos. Alternatively, listing all additional reading and videos upfront will allow the student to get some sort of idea of what's ahead, rather than thinking they're progressing at a decent pace and suddenly realizing that there's another 20 page article to read. This will help in planning our time and managing our effort and focus.

4) I'm still not sure I fully understand the links between ethics, strategy, risk management, corporate governance, governance structures, operating models etc. Although I think I have a vague grasp on the concepts holistically and have a general idea about it, I still struggle to articulate the distinctions and exactly how they relate to each other. This may be because of time constraints as I only managed about 20% of the additional required reading.

Feedback_Question: How did this course satisfy your initial expectations/needs?
Feedback_Response:
The content was well-structured and I enjoyed the online experience.  There were multiple errors in the revision and assignment questions however I understand that this was the first time that you run this course and the response to my queries was quick and effective and I appreciate this.  
Regrettably the exam was not in line with my expectations and I predict that you will likely have a high failure rate. 
We were informed that "not all the questions would be multiple choice and that there would be longer questions similar to those in the discussion forum".  By saying "not all", it implies that the exam would be predominantly multiple choice questions which it was not, only 10% of the paper was made up of multiple-choice questions and some of these questions were very different from those in the assignment questions for example the Resource Based View question - the correct answer was so foreign to me that I chose Explicit knowledge assuming that it was a mistake.  Further to this, we were informed that if we knew the assignment questions content and the discussion forum content, that we would pass.  This was not the case as I knew the content and was completely blindsided in the exam.  With courses of these nature, there is typically a very structured guide on what you need to know in the exam in the form of a scope thus most of us assumed that the scope was know the assignment content and the discussion forum content, which was misguided.  You have asked us to answer 20 point questions without giving us the correct answer to start with.  If your expectation of students is to be able to answer 20 mark long questions in the exam, you need to ask these questions at the end of each module in order for students to prepare in that way.  By only asking multiple choice questions, you create an expectation of that.  Further to this, the discussion forum content would not result in 20 marks as far as I could see, a student cannot expect to sift through the comments of other students and then try and figure out what the correct 20 points would be.  I referred to Rob's comments and these would not have resulted in 20 points so I assumed it would be paragraph style longer questions similar to his answers.   
 Myself and my 3 colleagues will be held liable for the course fee of R13000 for our likely failure which is not a small amount of money.  Accordingly if I do fail I would like to know what the pass rate is so that I can motivate that my likely failure will not be as a result of a lack of effort.

The course would have even been better if we were being assessed on the concepts that we were learning in some form of formal assessment outside the class engagement and discussions, such as assignments or one test/exam at the end of the course. This would test our acknowledge and understanding and give one an opportunity to see based on the results whether or not they full understood the content that was covered. 

The other online course I have done was the Bookkeeping course through GetSmarter. The weekly assignments were also quite extensive and difficult at times to manage given work and other personal commitments.

Feedback_Response:
Giving feedback on a course focused on critical systems thinking can indeed be challenging. The course material provided was extensive, covering a wide range of critical concepts and theories. The assignments for each module were well-constructed, effectively assessing my understanding of the content. However, there are a few areas where I believe improvements could be made to enhance the learning experience (just my personal opinion, of course).
Firstly, I believe that the inclusion of more practical examples within the study material would significantly benefit students in general, especially those who are more visual by nature, like myself. Whilst the theoretical content was comprehensive, it often felt quite dry and abstract. Being a very "visual" person, I sometimes found it challenging to translate these theoretical concepts into relatable, real-world applications.  The use of more practical examples would help bridge this gap, making the content more engaging and easier to grasp.
Interestingly, some of the assignments did incorporate practical "real-life" situations, which I found extremely valuable. These practical questions not only tested my understanding but also allowed me to see the direct application of theories in real-world scenarios. I would have liked to see more of these types of examples included in the study material itself, to provide a more balanced mix of theory and practice.
Additionally, the course emphasized the importance of reading for comprehension rather than simply skimming through passages. This was certainly a beneficial exercise, as it ensured that we truly understood the content rather than making assumptions. This approach added depth to my learning experience and is one aspect of the course that I found particularly important.
In conclusion, while the course was thorough and the assignments effectively reinforced the learning objectives, incorporating more practical examples within the study material would greatly enhance the overall learning experience. This would cater to different learning styles and make complex theoretical content more accessible and engaging.

Developing the core elements enhances one's ability to navigate the role better and effectively.
I have been mindful in establishing more regular and deliberate check-ins, feedback and input with my colleagues and sub-ordinates. Here the focus has been on the individuals, the team and the work product or problem statements/tasks.
The elements of socials skills presented were particularly useful in managing conflict or difficult scenarios with people and will continue to be so.
My role includes the big picture aspects of business and being more inclusive about this more regularly with a broader audience in the team, is very positive signs and is encouraging.

Feedback_Response:
Tools:

Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) Systems: Such as SAP, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics.
Supply Chain Management (SCM) Software: Including tools for demand forecasting, inventory management, and logistics planning.
Transportation Management Systems (TMS): For optimizing freight movements and logistics operations.
Warehouse Management Systems (WMS): To manage warehouse operations efficiently.
Inventory Optimization Tools: Like ABC analysis, EOQ (Economic Order Quantity), and safety stock calculations.
Data Analytics Tools: Such as Tableau, Power BI, or Python/R for data analysis and visualization in supply chain decision-making.

Techniques:

Lean Six Sigma: To identify and eliminate waste in processes.
Just-In-Time (JIT) Inventory Management: Minimizing inventory holding costs while meeting customer demand.
Total Quality Management (TQM): Continuous improvement of processes and products.
Demand Forecasting Techniques: Such as time-series analysis, causal methods, and collaborative forecasting.
Risk Management: Including techniques like SWOT analysis, scenario planning, and risk mitigation strategies.
Supplier Relationship Management (SRM): Strategies for managing supplier relationships and performance.

Concepts:

Logistics Network Design: Optimizing the structure of distribution networks.
Supply Chain Integration: Coordination and collaboration across supply chain partners.
Omni-channel Logistics: Fulfilling orders seamlessly across multiple channels (e.g., online, brick-and-mortar).
Green Logistics: Sustainable practices in logistics and supply chain operations.
Reverse Logistics: Managing the return of goods and materials.
International Logistics: Managing logistics activities across global supply chains, including customs regulations and international trade agreements.

Delivery:
The course delivery was no differently from subscribing to an expensive YouTube channel. The content was good in both quality and substance. From my perspective, it would have made no difference if you removed the lecturer and just shared the reading material. You may want to review the structure and approach of her involvement. I personally enrolled for engagements and accessing differing thoughts and view points from the others, not for the content - most of which I already has preview or access to. The Discussion forums were not discussions - I think we mostly complied to the requirement to participate rather that engaging on each other's thoughts. While that's not your issue, the structure of it lends itself to the same outcome, where each person just post their answers to the questions.

Questions and Assignments: 
I found the standard and structure of questions not to be appropriate for this level of study for the following two main reasons:
1. It emphases remembering of facts, and being correct, rather than encouraging critical thinking and application of the knowledge.
2. It emphases getting the correct answers  - that's agreeing with the examiner, not exploring alternative ways. There were many areas where I did not agree with the "correct" answers.

Points of consideration:
The course content is good and can be very useful if well applied. The majority of the content is already available in various platforms, and one does not have to pay R18k to access it and use it. I would however pay for the opportunity to develop the skills for critical thinking and application of the tools and knowledge from the course. To master the exploration of other views and ways of approaching problems and applying the tools to find solutions. There is more than one way to apply the tools in different contexts, not just what the examiner knows, thinks and believe. I believe participants will derive more value if they develop that skill, than to just know the facts. 

While an attempt is made to do so through reflections and discussion forums. I believe the questions and assignments should do more of this to improve the value of the course.
